summary: This document describes Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT), a protocol for delivering multicast traffic from sources in a multicast-enabled network to receivers that lack multicast connectivity to it. It uses UDP encapsulation and unicast replication to reach those receivers.

plainLanguage.summary: Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT) carries multicast data to a receiver that cannot reach the source network using native multicast. A gateway asks a relay to join the groups it needs, and the relay sends the traffic back inside UDP unicast packets; this costs more bandwidth than native multicast and does not provide strong security.

subtitle: Carries multicast traffic to gateways across networks that only provide unicast connectivity.

tldr.problem: Receivers may lack multicast connectivity to a network that carries the multicast sources they want to receive.
tldr.mechanism: An AMT gateway discovers a relay, exchanges encapsulated IGMP or MLD membership messages, and receives multicast datagrams over UDP unicast tunnels.
tldr.outcome: AMT extends multicast access across unicast-only links, but relays replicate traffic and the protocol does not provide strong security or congestion control. RFC 7450 is updated by RFCs 8777 and 9601.

today: RFC 7450 is a Proposed Standard for AMT and is updated by RFC 8777 and RFC 9601.

sections.title: Multicast over a Unicast Network
sections.content:
Multicast lets a source send one stream to receivers that have joined a group. Some receivers do not have multicast connectivity to the source network because of provider policy or network limitations.

AMT uses UDP encapsulation to bridge this gap. It supports Source-Specific Multicast and Any-Source Multicast, but is not intended to replace native multicast when traffic volumes are high because the relay sends separate unicast copies to gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: AMT carries a multicast stream to a receiver across a network that only forwards unicast traffic. The relay makes a separate copy for each gateway, so this method can use more bandwidth than native multicast.

sections.title: Gateways and Relays
sections.content:
The gateway sits near receivers without native multicast access. It uses the host side of Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) or Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) to track what receivers request.

The relay sits in a multicast-enabled network. It acts on membership updates, joins the required multicast traffic, and encapsulates incoming multicast datagrams for interested gateways. AMT itself handles the discovery, message exchange, encapsulation, and decapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway collects the receiver's group requests; the relay connects those requests to the multicast source network. They exchange control messages and multicast data over unicast UDP.

sections.title: Finding a Relay
sections.content:
A gateway needs a relay's unicast address before it can request multicast data. It can use a configured address or send a Relay Discovery message to an anycast discovery address.

A relay answers with a Relay Advertisement that echoes the discovery nonce and supplies its unicast address. The gateway checks the nonce and then sends later requests to that relay. Anycast routing can direct discovery to a nearby relay.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway can send a discovery message to an anycast address to find a nearby relay. The reply includes the relay's unicast address, which the gateway uses for later exchanges.

sections.title: Joining Groups and Receiving Data
sections.content:
The gateway periodically sends a Request to solicit a Membership Query from the relay. The query contains an encapsulated IGMP or MLD query; the gateway processes it and sends a Membership Update describing its group membership.

The relay uses updates to manage multicast forwarding state, then sends requested multicast datagrams in Multicast Data messages. A Teardown message can end delivery, while periodic requests and updates refresh membership and any NAT mapping along the path.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway asks the relay for a membership query, then reports which multicast groups its receivers want. The relay forwards matching multicast data until the gateway leaves the groups or tears down the tunnel.

sections.title: Security and Network Limits
sections.content:
AMT relies on UDP, IGMP, and MLD and does not provide confidentiality, general message integrity, or reliable delivery. Its handshake offers limited source authentication for allocating relay state, but does not stop eavesdropping or man-in-the-middle attacks.

AMT also lacks congestion control. Providers are expected to place relays near their network borders and limit which gateways can reach them; relay and gateway implementations should validate message contents and manage resource use.
sections.plainLanguage: AMT does not encrypt multicast requests or data, and it cannot prevent an attacker from changing traffic in transit. It also has no congestion control, so relay placement and access limits matter.
